title: preemptive-qos-degradation-and-scheduler-imbalances-incident-diary
content:
Executive summary:

On 2025-11-17 we observed a ~40% increase in P95 API latency for our hosted inference control plane and a correlated surge of pod backoffs in two clusters (us-west2-prod-a, us-west2-prod-b). Impact window ~2025-11-17T03:12Z -> 2025-11-17T04:08Z. Root cause: sudden bursty CI-driven workload + flawed kernel memory reclaim interplay on a set of older 8-GPU nodes causing QoS-classified Pods (Guaranteed vs BestEffort) to have disproportionate eviction/backoff behaviors and exposing a scheduler imbalance where continuous evictions overloaded the scheduler queue. This doc captures detection, live debugging, mitigations performed, an initial runbook draft for future incidents, and action items.

What made this unusual:
- The incident originated from a predictable source (CI job ramp) but manifested as prolonged scheduler imbalance because of kernel-level page reclaim behavior on nodes with mixed NUMA and memory cgroup settings.
- Metrics showed node memory pressure oscillating without full OOMKills; kubelet issued eviction hints repeatedly which kept pods in Terminating/Backoff loops rather than cleanly freeing resources.
- Standard node-pressure alerts (memory.available) fired, but our default automation scaled workloads horizontally in the same AZ, worsening local rack saturation.

Timeline (UTC):
- 03:06: alerting pipeline detected elevated pod backoff rate in us-west2-prod-a (> 120/min).
- 03:09: SRE on-call notified via pager. Initial dashboard P95 API latency jump identified.
- 03:12: Cluster autoscaler logs show simultaneous scale-up attempts; however several scale-ups failed due to AZ pinning and node startup quota throttle.
- 03:18: Node kernel log (dmesg) excerpt from gpu-node-17 shows repeated "kswapd0" activity and 'zone reclaim' warnings.
- 03:23: Kubelet logs on affected nodes show repeated eviction thresholds reached: "eviction manager: trying to reclaim memory" but memory reclaim incomplete.
- 03:28: We temporarily cordoned the three worst nodes and drained lowest-priority pods -> transient improvement.
- 03:32: Scheduler queue length peaked at 18k pending pods. Manual admission-rate throttling (ingress) applied to CI runners at 03:40 to stop new pod flood.
- 04:02: Kernel upgrade on older node family rolled out to test pool (reboot planned), but immediate fix was conservative: taint older nodes with "sre/qos-protect=enabled:NoSchedule" to avoid scheduling BestEffort/ Bursty CI pods there.
- 04:08: Incident declared mitigated.

Detection and observable signals:
- Alerts: pod_backoff_rate, node_memory_pressure (warn), scheduler_pending_count_high.
- Correlated metrics: node_memory_available dropped ~60% on three nodes; dmesg logs showed high kswapd activity but few OOM events. kubelet eviction manager logs show repetitive soft-eviction decisions on best-effort pods.
- Traces: request traces showed queueing at the control-plane ingress and long wait for model load init due to pod creation latency.

Live debugging artifacts (commands used):
- kubectl get nodes -o wide --show-labels | grep gpu
- ssh gpu-node-17 sudo dmesg | tail -n 100
- kubectl describe node gpu-node-17
- journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 | grep eviction
- kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}\t{.spec.nodeName}\n{end}' | wc -l
- jq '.items | length' pending-pods.json (saved list of pending pods at peak)

Key log excerpts (scrubbed):
- "eviction manager: eviction threshold reached, reclaiming memory, target reclaim 512MB"
- "kswapd0: high watermark reached, scanning zone, pages reclaimed insufficient"
- "kube-scheduler: scheduling attempt failed: insufficient memory, node had transient watermarks"

Root cause analysis (top-level):
1) Primary: Node-local kernel memory reclaim behavior on older instance types caused long stalls in freeing pages under a burst allocation pattern. Because the nodes are GPU-heavy with modest host memory tuning, kswapd activity prolonged and kubelet's eviction manager repeatedly made soft eviction decisions without reclaiming enough memory to stabilize workloads.
2) Secondary: A CI workload pattern (large ephemeral test runner pods ramping up) created a concentrated burst of BestEffort pods in a small AZ because CI runners were not globally distributed; autoscaler decisions and AZ pinning amplified the contention.
3) Tertiary: Scheduling failure amplification: when pods were repeatedly evicted/Backoff, the scheduler queue ballooned; the scheduler's default backoff and prioritization semantics meant Guaranteed pods eventually progressed but BestEffort pods suffered long tail latencies impacting control-plane tasks that had BestEffort components (e.g., sidecars).

Why existing mitigations were insufficient:
- Node cordon/drain helped but was reactive and slow compared to the pace of pod churn.
- Autoscaler increased capacity but hit cloud quota/az pinning, delaying node availability.
- No existing node tainting for older instance types to prevent bursty, non-critical pods from landing on them.

Immediate mitigations applied during incident:
- Cordoned and drained three nodes (gpu-node-17/18/19).
- Tainted older node pool to avoid BestEffort/CI pods: kubectl taint nodes <node> sre/qos-protect=enabled:NoSchedule
- Throttled CI ingress via the CI controller to limit concurrent new job spawns (in-flight jobs < 30 per-AZ).
- Temporarily bumped kube-scheduler --max-acceptable-pending=5000 (note: runtime knob used carefully).
- Opened emergency cloud quota ticket to speed up node creation; escalated to infra on-call.

Follow-up permanent actions (proposed):
- Short-term (2 weeks):
  - Add node tainting rule for old-instance-family: avoid scheduling BestEffort and bursty CI workloads there. Owner: Lin Zhao. Due: 2025-11-30.
  - Update CI runner placement strategy to distribute across AZs and prefer larger host-memory node types when GPU is required. Owner: Diego Martinez. Due: 2025-12-08.
  - Add an alert that combines kswapd high activity + node memory oscillation to detect kernel reclaim pathology earlier. Owner: Asha Patel. Due: 2025-12-01.
- Medium-term (1–2 months):
  - Evaluate kernel tuning options and memory cgroup knobs for GPU-heavy nodes; run a staged kernel patch and test plan. Owner: infra-kernel-team (Priya Nair). Due: 2026-01-15.
  - Scheduler tuning: investigate backoff thresholds and admission throttles to avoid 10k+ pending backlog scenarios. Owner: eng-sre. Due: 2026-01-30.
- Long-term (Q1 2026):
  - Replace older 8-GPU node pools with modern node types that have larger host memory and NUMA-balanced layouts. Owner: platform-engineering. Due: 2026-03-31.

Runbook draft: "qos-degradation-scheduler-overload" (initial steps):
1) Detect:
   - If pod_backoff_rate > 100/min and scheduler_pending_count > 2k for > 5m, page SRE on-call and create incident channel.
2) Triage:
   - Determine if the spike is caused by an intentional deploy/CI ramp. Check CI controller > recent job starts.
   - Run: kubectl top nodes; watch node_memory_available metric for high variance.
3) Contain:
   - Temporarily throttle CI ingestion (config flag in CI controller).
   - Cordon nodes with sustained kswapd activity, drain BestEffort pods first: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector='qos=BestEffort'.
   - If node creation is queued, escalate cloud quota and consider cross-AZ redistribution of pods.
4) Mitigate:
   - Apply taint: sre/qos-protect=enabled:NoSchedule to older node families.
   - If scheduler queue > 5k, reduce new admissions by flipping admission controller flag for non-critical namespaces.
5) Recover:
   - After steady state for 20m, uncordon nodes one at a time and monitor kswapd and node_memory_available.
6) Postmortem:
   - Capture pending pod list, kubelet logs, dmesg; store in incident artifact bucket; run RCA within 2 weeks.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why did kswapd activity not result in OOM kills? (expected fallback is OOM). Hypothesis: host memory pressure was mitigated by reclaim but not fast enough to reflect in oom_kill metrics. Need kernel-level tracing.
- Could we proactively detect "kswapd stall" patterns via node-exporter? Need to instrument /proc/vmstat heuristics.
- Is there a scheduler-side rate limiter we can add that differentiates BestEffort versus Guaranteed for backoff policy?

Post-incident tasks (owners & tentative due dates):
- Capture full kubelet and dmesg log bundle for affected nodes -> place in S3 incident-bundles/2025-11-17/gpu-node-17.tar.gz. Owner: Diego Martinez. Due: 2025-11-20.
- Implement node tainting policy for old-instance-family in staging and run chaos test (draining BestEffort pods) -> Owner: Lin Zhao. Due: 2025-11-30.
- Create CI placement limitation PR and add integration test to ensure AZ distribution -> Owner: Diego Martinez. PR: github.com/redwood-inference/ci/PR-298. Due: 2025-12-08.
- Design and run kernel reclaim microbenchmark across node types -> Owner: Priya Nair. Due: 2026-01-10.

Communications:
- Notified platform team and CI owners immediately. Drafted customer-facing summary for impacted customers (control-plane latency blip), reviewed by SRE lead.
- Internal postmortem scheduled: 2025-11-25 16:00 UTC.

Appendix: monitoring queries and example alerts
- pod_backoff_rate: sum by(cluster) (increase(rate(kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason{reason=~"BackOff"}[5m]))) > 100
- scheduler_pending_count_high: count(kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Pending"}) > 2000
- kswapd_indicator (prometheus): rate(node_vmstat_pgscan_kswapd[1m]) > threshold && rate(node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes[1m]) is decreasing rapidly

Notes to self (scratchpad):
- Re-check if gpu-node family had a custom sysctl set for vm.swappiness in 2024 migration.
- Add a synthetic test that ramps 50 burst pods in canary AZ to validate scheduler behavior.

End of incident diary.

(Feel free to edit this doc into a lighter postmortem or to copy relevant runbook steps into the canonical runbooks space.)
